newsitem.title: USA: House committee passes $13 bln lands spending bill.
newsitem.headline: House committee passes $13 bln lands spending bill.

text.p: The House Appropriations Committee Thursday passed a $13 billion spending bill on energy, lands and Indian programmes for the 1998 fiscal year.

The budget for the Interior Department and fossil fuel energy projects at the Energy Department was $100 million less than the Clinton administration requested and $500 million less than Congress approved for 1997, but 1997 funding included more than $600 million in emergency spending.

Debate centred on two contentious issues -- funding for the National Endowment for the Arts, which most of the committee's Republicans voted to shut, and $700 million for land acquisitions that the committee excluded from the bill.

The committee provided only $10 million for the NEA, which Republicans said should be used to close the agency. Funding the NEA amounted to "the expropriation of taxpayers' dollars for elitist purposes," said committee chairman Bob Livingston, a Louisiana Republican.

Democrats failed to save the controversial agency when the committee rejected a proposal to sell $89 million worth of oil from the nation's emergency stockpile to help fund it at the same level as this year.

Representative David Obey of Wisconsin, the top Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, defended the NEA's record, saying that of more than 110,000 grants it issued for arts programmes around the country, only 45 had been "objectionable."
"This is a quintessential outreach operation that we should not squelch," he said.

The committee defeated a Democratic amendment to provide $65 million to pay off a company not to develop a gold mine on the edge of Yellowstone National Park and $250 million to trade land to save the Headwaters grove in California, the nation's largest remaining uncut old growth forest.

The two deals were negotiated by the White House and backed by many lawmakers but they were included in a $700 million package targeted exclusively for land buys in the administration's budget agreement with Congress, which the committee refused to endorse.
Interior appropriations panel chairman Ralph Regula, an Ohio Republican, said the money should be spent on maintaining the nation's parks instead of buying more land.

The bill provided $1.2 billion for running the national parks, $78 million more than this year. It also allocated $637 million for energy conservation programmes, up $67 million from 1997, $510 million for Indian education, up $28 million from this year, and $136 million for restoring the Everglades, up $79 million from this year.
